Chapter 28

A public API worth using

One error shape, a request id on every response, and the four bugs that curl found in an afternoon.

By the end of this chapter

Build the plumbing that makes every /api/v1 route behave the same way.

A browser and an algorithm want different things from the same venue, and pretending otherwise gives you an API that is bad at both. A person gets a redirect to a sign-in page; a trading system gets a 401 with a code it can branch on. A person sees a nicely designed error page; a trading system needs to know whether to retry.

The most valuable property of an API

It is not speed and it is not breadth. It is that the failures are as predictable as the successes. A client that knows exactly what a failure looks like can be written once and left alone. A client that has to guess grows a catch block full of string matching, and every copy-edit you make to an error message becomes an outage at somebody else's firm.

One error shape

  • code is what a machine reads. It never changes once published — it is as much a part of the contract as the URL itself.
  • message is for the human reading a log. It may change freely, which is exactly why nothing should branch on it.
  • requestId is in the body *and* in an X-Request-Id header, so a support conversation that starts with a screenshot can still find the log line.

Seven codes. Not seventy. Every one of them is something a client would genuinely handle differently: re-authenticate, give up, fix the request, back off, wait, or page somebody. If you cannot name the different action a client takes, it does not need its own code.

Why not SvelteKit's error()

The bug in the reverse map

Authorisation failures and feature-flag pauses are thrown with SvelteKit's error(status, message) deeper in the stack, so the API layer needs to translate a status back into a code. The first version was an if chain:

Then we added the venue-pause feature flag, which throws error(503, 'The venue is not accepting new orders at the moment. Cancels still work.'). The chain has no 503 branch, so it fell through to the last line, and pausing the venue told every API client "something went wrong at our end" — a 500, which clients treat as a bug to report rather than a state to wait out.

Derive, do not duplicate

The if chain and the status map held the same knowledge in two shapes, and only one of them got updated. Deriving the second from the first makes the class of bug impossible rather than merely fixed — nobody has to remember, because there is nothing to remember.

The handler wrapper

Every route is export const GET = handler(async ({ viewer }, { url }) => { … }). Without the wrapper, each +server.ts grows its own try/catch, they drift, and one of them eventually returns a stack trace containing a file path and a SQL statement to whoever asked for it.

Four bugs an afternoon of curl found

None of these were found by tests. All four were found by calling the API by hand, the way a new client would.

  1. The first order every API key placed was rejected. The gateway parsed the command *before* stamping the caller's identity onto it, so validation ran against an object with no firmId and answered Expected "firmId" but received undefined. Fixed by stamping first, then parsing.
  2. An unpinned API key resolved to zero accounts. accountsFor() looked up account_assignment by user id — and a key is not a user. Every key without a pinned account could authenticate and then trade nothing. Fixed with allAccountsOf(client, firmId).
  3. Every 401 and 429 carried requestId: "unknown". The id was minted after authentication. Fixed above.
  4. A body-less DELETE was refused as a cross-site form submission. That one got its own chapter in Part 4.

Be your own first client

Three of those four are invisible from inside the application, because the web UI takes a different path through the same code — it has a session, not a key, and it sends a body on every request. The single highest-value hour in this project was spent with curl and no test framework at all.

Checkpoint

  • You can state the fixed error shape and say which field a client is allowed to branch on
  • You can explain why error() is the wrong helper for a JSON API
  • You can explain why the reverse map is derived rather than written
  • You can explain why the request id is minted before authentication
